forces: Two violins, viola and two cellos
performers: Isaac Stern, Alexander Schneider, violins; Milton Katims, viola; Pablo Casals, Paul Tortelier, cellos
question: How does a calm melody survive a storm and return changed?
intro: The slow movement of Schubert’s last chamber work is a calm E major song for four players over a plucked cello, interrupted by a violent F minor storm. Casals and his Prades colleagues play it at a deliberate pace in a 1952 recording.

sections.label: A · E major, a plucked cello below
A′ · E major returns with running notes
sections.mNote: opening returns with running 32nd notes in the second cello

sections.label: Coda · F minor recalled, E major again

cues.title: Three held voices, a plucked cello
cues.text: The Adagio, in E major and 12/8, begins pianissimo. The first violin’s dotted figure and the second cello’s plucked pulse frame three sustained inner voices: second violin, viola and first cello. The writing is predominantly quiet, but forte swells already occur on the first page.
cues.evidence: The score (IMSLP #885759, printed p. 17) is headed Adagio, in four sharps, with pp in the first bars, the dotted figure in the first violin, three sustained inner parts, pizz. in the lowest staff, espressivo on one inner line and f swells later on the page. The report’s opening level is −27.7 dB at 0:00; no entry is timed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dotted figures, long lines
cues.text: Blumhofer’s programme note hears the opening as a dotted rhythm in the first violin, carried over from the first movement, accompanying a slowly unfolding melody in the lower strings. Listen for that quiet dotted pulse against the broad line below.
cues.evidence: Blumhofer’s note is quoted at length in John Buxton’s post (https://classicalguy.substack.com/p/building-a-collection-24-schuberts). The report shows a steady quiet level, −19.2 to −21.3 dB at 0:15–0:40, with 1.6–2.8 detected attacks per second. The score’s dotted figure in the first violin is visible on printed p. 17 (IMSLP #885759); the description is not timed.

cues.title: Two months before the end
cues.text: Schubert composed the Quintet in the summer or early autumn of 1828 and finished it in late September or early October, about two months before he died on 19 November. He offered it to the publisher Probst, who replied asking only for songs and more popular piano music.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s String Quintet (Schubert) article, “Composition and publication history”: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert). Probst replied asking to see some of Schubert’s vocal works and requesting more popular piano music.

cues.title: The first paragraph lifts
cues.text: A boundary at about 1:42 marks the end of the movement’s first long paragraph: the key estimates, which have rested on F♯ and B for a minute, move briefly towards A and E. The line reaches upward and then settles again.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 1:42 (novelty 0.54); local key reads F♯ major at 0:40–1:30 (r 0.89–0.98) then B major at 1:40 (0.83) and A major at 1:50 (0.84). The estimates fix on dominant-side notes, which the long phrases dwell on; no chord is identified.

cues.title: Listen for what returns
cues.text: The paragraph that runs from about 2:15 to 4:02 will come back closely, a little under eight minutes later. Keep its shape in mind: the long-breathed line sinking to a hush at 2:15 and 2:25, among the quietest windows of the movement.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 135.5–242.0 s with 613.5–720.0 s (offset 478 s, no transposition, similarity 0.95); the quietest windows include 2:15 (−27.1 dB) and 2:25 (−25.3 dB).

cues.title: Rubinstein’s wish
cues.text: The Adagio is one of the most loved slow movements in chamber music. Wikipedia records that the pianist Arthur Rubinstein wished to have it played at his funeral, and that the violinist John Saunders had the Quintet’s first-movement second theme carved on his tombstone.

cues.title: Into B minor and back
cues.text: Around 3:00 the key estimate darkens briefly to B minor, a tentative reading, and E major is read again by about 3:40, staying until the section’s close. The tonic is approached slowly, not announced.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 3:00 (0.62); local key reads B minor at 3:00 (r 0.57), E major at 3:10 (0.73), A major at 3:20 (0.83) and E major at 3:40–4:00 (r 0.91–0.95). These are estimates, the B minor reading has low confidence, and no chord or bar is identified.

cues.title: The storm breaks
cues.text: At 4:30, after a hush, the music bursts into F minor, a semitone above the tonic, fortissimo. The relationship of E major to F minor, the flat supertonic, will be exploited in the movements that follow. The second cello’s pluck is swept away.
cues.evidence: The strongest boundary in the report is 4:30 (novelty 1.00): level rises from −23.3 dB at 4:20 to −8.4 dB at 4:30, with a local key of F minor at 4:30–4:40 and 4:50 (r 0.68–0.82). The score (IMSLP #885759, p. 18) shows ff, fz accents and a change to four flats. The relation to later movements is stated in Wikipedia’s article.

cues.title: A duet in the storm
cues.text: Blumhofer hears the turbulent middle section as marked by an impassioned duet between first violin and first cello. The loudest windows of the whole recording are near 5:20, 5:45, 6:10 and 6:40, all inside this storm.
cues.evidence: The loudest windows are 6:35, 6:10, 6:40, 5:20 and 5:45 (−6.0 dB at 5:20, −4.1 dB at 6:10, −4.5 dB at 6:40); boundaries at 5:52 (0.53) and 6:04 (0.56). Blumhofer’s description is quoted in the Buxton post; the duet is not timed.

cues.title: Not heard in his lifetime
cues.text: Schubert never heard the Quintet played in public. The first known performance was on 17 November 1850 at the Musikverein in Vienna; it was published in 1853, and the manuscript and sketches are now lost.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s String Quintet (Schubert) article: the work remained unpublished at Schubert’s death, the first known public performance was on 17 November 1850, and publication followed in 1853 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_Quintet_(Schubert)).

cues.title: The storm subsides
cues.text: By about 7:20 the storm has gone. The score marks a diminuendo into ppp and very quiet, separated chords and fragments before the key signature changes back to four sharps. The recording’s quietest window of the second half comes at 7:40.
cues.evidence: Level falls from −15.2 dB at 7:00 to −24.8 dB at 7:20 and −25.4 dB at 7:40, with 3.4 to 5.0 detected attacks per second at 7:30–7:50, which does not show how the notes are played; the boundary is 7:20 (0.60). The score (IMSLP #885759, printed pp. 21–22) shows dim., then ppp and quiet separated chords before the key signature changes back to four sharps.

cues.title: E major comes back
cues.text: At about 7:58 the opening returns in E major, with a running 32nd-note passage in the second cello that seems to grow out of the turbulence before it. The recording matches the earlier music for more than a minute and a half.
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 135.5–242.0 s with 613.5–720.0 s (offset 478 s) and 238.5–266.0 s with 718.0–745.5 s; boundaries at 9:44 (0.69), 10:48 (0.61) and 11:16 (0.59) echo those at about 1:46, 2:48 and 3:18. The 32nd-note passage is Wikipedia’s description; the first bar of the return is not aligned.

cues.title: Casals at Prades
cues.text: Casals lived in exile at Prades in France from 1939 and in 1950 resumed his career at the festival there. The LP sleeve says Columbia recorded this quintet at the 1952 festival, with Stern, Schneider, Katims and Tortelier; John Buxton dates it to July. It was issued in 1953.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pablo Casals article (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Casals) for Prades and 1950; the sleeve notes, read as the Internet Archive’s OCR text (https://archive.org/download/lp_casals-festival-at-prades-third-series-qui_franz-schubert-isaac-stern-alexander-schne/lp_casals-festival-at-prades-third-series-qui_franz-schubert-isaac-stern-alexander-schne_djvu.txt), for the Casals Festival of 1952 in Prades and the five players; John Buxton’s post (https://classicalguy.substack.com/p/building-a-collection-24-schuberts) for the month of July; the Internet Archive item for the 1953 release.

cues.title: A reviewer on the grunting
cues.text: John Buxton, recommending this recording, notes that if you listen closely you will hear Casals’s grunting in several places, and that the playing is not immaculate. For him the musicality, emotion and elan outweigh the flaws.
cues.evidence: John Buxton’s post notes Casals’s audible grunting in this recording and that the playing is not immaculate (https://classicalguy.substack.com/p/building-a-collection-24-schuberts); the observation covers the recording as a whole and no instance is timed here.

cues.title: The last swell
cues.text: From about 10:15 to 12:00 the returning section matches the first section’s second half closely. Near 11:10 it swells to −9.3 dB, about four decibels louder than the same stretch the first time, at 3:10 (−14.0 dB).
cues.evidence: A recurrence analysis matches 135.5–242.0 s with 613.5–720.0 s (similarity 0.95). Level is −9.3 dB at 11:10 (E major, r 0.85) and −14.0 dB at 3:10 (E major, r 0.73), the corresponding stretch 478 s earlier; boundaries at 10:48 (0.61) and 11:16 (0.59). Levels are relative within this recording.

cues.title: F minor, then E major
cues.text: Near 12:30 the level peaks at about −11 dB and then falls away, and the report reads E major from 12:50. Wikipedia says the last three measures modulate to the F minor of the middle section and return at once to E major; the bars cannot be aligned from the level alone.
cues.evidence: Boundaries at 12:28 (0.77) and 12:46 (0.74); level −11.0 dB at 12:30, then −23.1 dB at 12:40; local key E major at 12:50–13:00 (r 0.86, 0.90). The F minor–E major close is Wikipedia’s description of the last three measures, on the final system of the Adagio on printed p. 25 (IMSLP #885759, above the start of the Scherzo). The recording is not aligned to bars, and the level peak is not identified with a particular chord.

transitions.title: A semitone up, fortissimo
transitions.from: A · E major, a plucked cello below
transitions.how: After the tranquil first section, in E major, the music breaks off and enters F minor a semitone above, fortissimo. The score adds fz accents and fast triplet figures, and the second cello’s plucked pulse gives way to driving bowed notes. There is no pivot chord: the shock of a distant key is the join. The same E major to F minor relation returns in later movements.
transitions.evidence: Level rises from −23.3 dB at 4:20 to −8.4 dB at 4:30; boundary 4:30 (novelty 1.00); local key reads F minor at 4:30–4:50. The accents, triplets and key change are read from the score (IMSLP #885759, p. 18); the relation to later movements is in Wikipedia. Bars are not aligned.

transitions.title: Down to ppp, then the opening
transitions.to: A′ · E major returns with running notes
transitions.how: The storm falls away through a diminuendo to ppp, with quiet, separated chords and fragments, and the key signature returns to four sharps. The opening music then returns in E major, and the second cello adds a running 32nd-note passage that, Wikipedia suggests, seems motivated by the preceding turbulence. The harmony is the same as the first time through, but a restless low voice now colours it.
transitions.evidence: Level falls from −15.2 dB at 7:00 to −25.4 dB at 7:40, with 3.4–5.0 detected attacks per second at 7:30–7:50; a recurrence analysis matches the first section with an offset of 478 s. The attack rate does not show how the notes are played. The score (IMSLP #885759, printed pp. 21–22) shows dim., ppp, quiet separated chords and the change of key signature; the 32nd-note passage is Wikipedia’s description.

transitions.title: The storm’s key, once more
transitions.from: A′ · E major returns with running notes
transitions.to: Coda · F minor recalled, E major again
transitions.how: In the last three measures Schubert modulates to the F minor of the middle section and returns at once to E major. The movement thus ends by reminding the listener of what it has passed through, then settling. The relation is the flat supertonic, which the third and fourth movements exploit. The recording’s level falls after the peak at about 12:30 and the report reads E major again from 12:50.
transitions.evidence: Boundaries at 12:28 (0.77) and 12:46 (0.74); level −11.0 dB at 12:30 and −23.1 dB at 12:40, with E major at 12:50–13:00. The modulation to F minor and the return to E major in the last three measures are Wikipedia’s description, on the final system of the Adagio on printed p. 25 of the score (IMSLP #885759); the audio is not aligned to bars.

source.title: Schubert, Streichquintett C-dur, Franz Schubert’s Werke, Serie IV No. 1 (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, 1890, plate F.S. 22)
source.locator: IMSLP #885759, II. Adagio, printed pp. 17–25 (the last three bars are on p. 25, above the start of the Scherzo). The “cellos” section stands for both cellos; the second cello’s pizzicato and running notes are noted where they matter. Timings follow the boundaries and the recurrence analysis and are approximate.

timeline.note: Three sustained inner voices, pianissimo, between the first violin’s dotted figure and the plucked second cello.
F minor storm: fortissimo, with a duet of first violin and first cello that Blumhofer describes.
The storm subsides into ppp chords and fragments.
E major returns; the second cello adds running 32nd notes.
The last bars recall F minor and settle in E major.

composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind
More than 600 songs; symphonies, chamber music, piano sonatas and duets, masses and music for the stage
composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.
